title: Single-cell-level distributions and relationships can differentiate cell-division and growth models
abstract: Complex interactions among regulatory molecules determine the rules underlying cell growth and division in microbial cells. While the governing molecular network may not always be obvious, it is well known that correlations among certain physiological quantities measured in experiments, such as birth-size, division-size, division-time, and division-added-size, can differentiate among various cell-division models, such as Timer, Sizer, and Adder. Here we show that, apart from these correlations, which we extend for the case of stochastic single-cell growth and stochastic asymmetric partitioning, probability distributions of these quantities and statistical relationships between them can also be used to differentiate between these division models. Interestingly, we show that these quantities can not only differentiate the division models, but also distinguish among the single-cell growth paradigms, such as linear and exponential growth. We then demonstrate this differentiability among various division and growth models by comparing our analytical results with published experimental data. We further show that these results remain valid even when the growth rate of a cell is correlated with the growth rate of cells from previous generations in the lineage.
summary: This work uses advanced statistical methods to analyze single-cell measurements from bacterial growth. By examining probability distributions and correlations among size and time metrics, the authors demonstrate that one can uniquely determine whether cell division follows a Timer, Sizer, or Adder rule, and whether the underlying growth is linear or exponential. This provides a powerful diagnostic tool for understanding fundamental biophysical processes.
main_problem: The study aims to differentiate between various underlying cell-division (e.g., Sizer, Adder) and single-cell growth models (linear vs. exponential) in microbial cells.
main_result: Analysis of probability distributions, statistical relationships (especially involving standard deviations), and correlations among single-cell quantities can uniquely distinguish between different division and growth mechanisms.
method: The authors derive analytical probability distributions and statistical moments for key observables by assuming various underlying mechanistic models. These theoretical predictions are then compared against published experimental data.
model_or_system: The physical system is bacterial cell growth and division, modeled using concepts like Timer, Sizer, and Adder mechanisms. The analysis extends to stochastic single-cell growth and asymmetric partitioning.
key_observables: Single-cell quantities: birth-size ($s_b$), division-size ($s_d$), division-time ($	au_d$), and division-added-size ($\Delta d$). Statistical measures include probability distributions, means, standard deviations, and correlation coefficients.
important_parameters: Growth rate autocorrelation parameters ($\alpha$, $ eta$); temperature variations (e.g., $25^\circ	ext{C}, 37^\circ	ext{C}$); partitioning fraction ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes independence between certain variables (like growth rate and size parameters) or relies on approximations like assuming sharply spiked distributions for moment calculations.
figures_summary: Figures compare experimental single-cell distributions ($s_b, s_d, \Delta d, 	au_d$) against analytical predictions from various model combinations. Plots of correlations (PCC) are used to test the consistency of different models across multiple temperatures.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing that simple correlations are insufficient, then showing how full probability distributions and statistical relationships (means vs. standard deviations) provide stronger discriminative power between division/growth models, culminating in comparisons with experimental data.
why_interesting: While the subject is biology, the rigorous application of stochastic processes, moment analysis, and distribution fitting to distinguish underlying physical laws mirrors techniques used in analyzing complex non-equilibrium systems in statistical mechanics.
